practiceSet.title: U1.LT4 Practice: Communicating Experimental Data
practiceSet.description: Practice choosing the right graph, setting up axes, titles, and units, reading data tables, finding the mean, describing trends, and writing a CER.

activity.title: U1.LT4 Relearning: Communicating Experimental Data
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can communicate data and information from a scientific experiment in a concise way.

**Think of a sports highlight reel.** Nobody wants to rewatch every second of every game. A highlight reel shows what mattered, fast. A good data table, graph, and CER do the same for an experiment: they show the results clearly so anyone can understand them quickly.

**Data tables:** a complete data table has a descriptive **title**, the **variables** as column headings, **(units)** for each variable, and lines drawn with a straight edge. Put the **IV in the left column** and the **DV in the right column**.

**Choosing a graph:**
- **Line graph:** the most common science graph; shows how the DV changes as the IV changes (like over time).
- **Bar chart:** compares separate groups or categories (kinds of pets, brands of sneakers); gaps between bars.
- **Histogram:** continuous data in ranges (student heights in ranges: 150–159 cm, 160–169 cm, ...); no gaps between bars.
- **Pie chart:** percents of a whole.
- **Scatter plot:** individual data points, to look for a pattern.

**Building a line graph:** (1) Identify the variables: **IV on the x-axis (horizontal), DV on the y-axis (vertical)**. (2) Determine the scale: equal spacing, using most of the graph. (3) Number and label each axis **with units**. (4) Plot the data points. (5) Draw a **best-fit line** (not connect-the-dots). (6) Title the graph so it clearly tells what it is about, naming both variables. One common format is DV vs. IV, like "Number of Leaves vs. Hours of Light." A graph with more than one data set needs a **key**.

**Reading trends:** **Directly proportional:** as the IV increases, the DV increases. **Inversely proportional:** as the IV increases, the DV decreases. **Interpolate:** predict a value between two measured points. **Extrapolate:** extend the graph beyond the measured data (riskier, because the trend may not continue).

**Mean:** add all the values, then divide by how many values there are. The mean of several trials is more reliable than one trial.

**CER template:** **Problem Statement** → **Claim** (in one sentence, the answer to the problem statement) → **Evidence** (data tables and/or graphs) → **Evidence writing** (explain how your data supports your claim; summarize your data into 3 statements: trends, patterns) → **Reasoning** (explain why your evidence supports your claim, using science ideas and vocabulary) → **Reflection** (one thing you learned, possible experimental errors, and additional experiments that could be done).

**Worked example 1:** Heart rates after drinking root beer: 80, 78, 83, and 79 beats per minute. Find the mean. Step 1: Add: 80 + 78 + 83 + 79 = 320. Step 2: Divide by the number of values: 320 ÷ 4 = **80 beats per minute**.

**Worked example 2:** Choose the graph. (a) Deer harvested in Chippewa County each day of gun season: the count changes over time, so use a **line graph**. (b) Number of students who own each kind of pet: separate categories, so use a **bar chart**. (c) Percent of the class with each eye color: parts of a whole, so use a **pie chart**.

**Worked example 3:** Problem: Do pill bugs prefer damp or dry soil? Data: in 5 trials, a mean of 8 out of 10 pill bugs ended on the damp side and 2 ended on the dry side. **Claim:** Pill bugs prefer damp soil over dry soil. **Evidence:** In 5 trials, a mean of 8 of 10 pill bugs (80%) ended on the damp side, and only 2 (20%) ended on the dry side. **Reasoning:** Pill bugs breathe with gill-like structures that must stay moist, so damp places help them survive. **Reflection:** One side may have been brighter than the other; next time we would keep the light the same on both sides.

**Watch out for:** putting the IV on the y-axis; leaving off units; titles that don't name the variables ("My Graph"); connect-the-dots lines; unequal spacing on an axis; using a line graph for categories; dividing by the wrong number when finding a mean; a claim that is longer than one sentence; evidence with no numbers; and mixing up evidence (the data) with reasoning (the why).
prompts: A student measured heart rate after 0, 5, 10, and 15 minutes of exercise: 70, 95, 115, and 130 beats per minute. Describe how you would set up a line graph: what goes on each axis, the units, and the title. Then describe the trend.
Find the mean of these trial times: 14 s, 16 s, 15 s, and 17 s. Then explain why scientists use the mean of several trials instead of one trial.

Choose the best graph for each data set and explain why: (a) percent of students with each blood type, (b) the number of students whose test scores fall in each 10-point range, (c) the height of a sunflower measured every week.
Write a complete CER for this problem: Do pill bugs prefer light or dark areas? Data: in 5 trials, a mean of 9 out of 10 pill bugs ended on the dark side and 1 ended on the light side.
